items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "pluripotent"?
options: Describes a stem cell that can form a limited range of cell types (e.g. bone marrow stem cells forming blood cells).
A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled mitosis.
Describes a stem cell that can form almost any cell type of the body (e.g. embryonic stem cells).
A factor or substance that causes cancer, such as tar, UV light or ionising radiation.
items.answer: Describes a stem cell that can form almost any cell type of the body (e.g. embryonic stem cells).
items.markingKey: Pluripotent: describes a stem cell that can form almost any cell type of the body (e.g. embryonic stem cells).

items.stem: State why water-soluble signalling molecules cannot enter the cell.
items.answer: They are polar / large and cannot cross the hydrophobic bilayer, so they bind to receptors on the surface.
items.markingKey: They are polar / large and cannot cross the hydrophobic bilayer, so they bind to receptors on the surface [1]

items.stem: A student in Singapore states: "Antibiotics can be used to control the spread of measles." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Measles is caused by a virus; antibiotics do not affect viruses. Vaccination controls it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Measles is caused by a virus; antibiotics do not affect viruses. Vaccination controls it. [2]

items.answer: High CO₂ reduces the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, so more oxygen is released.

Which genetic material can be found in viruses?
options: DNA or RNA, but not both
items.answer: DNA or RNA, but not both

items.stem: Which part of an antibody gives it its specificity?
items.answer: The variable region
items.markingKey: Its amino acid sequence determines the shape of the antigen-binding site.

items.stem: An enzyme reaction rate doubles between 20 °C and 30 °C. What is the Q10?
items.markingKey: Q10 = rate at (T + 10) ÷ rate at T.

items.stem: A person breathes 18 times per minute with a tidal volume of 0.5 dm³. What is the pulmonary ventilation rate?
items.answer: 9 dm³ min⁻¹
items.markingKey: 0.5 × 18 = 9 dm³ min⁻¹.

items.stem: Omar writes in a revision note: "Sieve tube elements are dead cells like xylem vessels." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Sieve tube elements are living but have no nucleus; they depend on companion cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Sieve tube elements are living but have no nucleus; they depend on companion cells. [2]

items.stem: The diploid number of an onion is 16. Copy and complete the table to show the number of chromosomes, chromatids (where chromosomes have two) and DNA molecules in one cell at: G1, G2, metaphase, and in each daughter nucleus at the end of telophase.
items.answer: G1: 16 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules (single chromatids). G2: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids, 32 DNA molecules. Metaphase: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids, 32 DNA. Telophase (each nucleus): 16 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules.
items.markingKey: one mark per correct stage [4]

items.stem: What is the name for "the contribution of dissolved solutes to water potential; always negative"?
items.answer: Solute potential (ψs)
items.markingKey: Solute potential (ψs): the contribution of dissolved solutes to water potential; always negative.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "the number of people with a disease at a particular time in a population"?
items.answer: Prevalence
items.markingKey: Prevalence: the number of people with a disease at a particular time in a population.

items.stem: A student in Mexico City states: "All mutations are harmful." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Many mutations are neutral (e.g. silent) and some are beneficial.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Many mutations are neutral (e.g. silent) and some are beneficial. [2]

items.stem: The R–R interval on an ECG recorded at 25 mm s⁻¹ is 20 mm. What is the heart rate?
items.answer: 75 beats min⁻¹

items.stem: Explain how the ice is less dense than liquid water of water is important to living organisms.
items.answer: Ice floats and insulates the water below, so aquatic organisms survive in winter; hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open lattice in ice.
items.markingKey: importance [1]; explained by hydrogen bonding / dipoles [1] [2]

items.answer: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. [2]

items.stem: Omar examined a stained blood smear and counted 250 white blood cells: neutrophils 138, lymphocytes 63, monocytes 11, others 38. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of neutrophils and lymphocytes. (b) The total white cell count is 8 × 10⁹ dm⁻³. Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³. (c) Describe how you would distinguish a neutrophil from a lymphocyte in the smear.
items.answer: (a) neutrophils 55.2%; lymphocytes 25.2% (b) 4.42 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (c) Neutrophil: lobed nucleus, granular cytoplasm, larger (10–12 μm). Lymphocyte: large round nucleus filling most of the cell, little cytoplasm, smaller (about 7 μm).
items.markingKey: (a) 138 ÷ 250 × 100 = 55.2% [1]; 63 ÷ 250 × 100 = 25.2% [1] (b) 0.552 × 8 × 10⁹ = 4.42 × 10⁹ [2] (c) neutrophil lobed nucleus [1]; lymphocyte large round nucleus / little cytoplasm [1] [6]

items.answer: (a) 40 μmol min⁻¹ (b) 2 mmol dm⁻³
items.markingKey: (a) 80 ÷ 2 = 40 [1] (b) substrate concentration at rate 40 = 2 mmol dm⁻³ [1] [2]

items.answer: Gas exchange happens across alveolar walls.

items.answer: DNA replication happens in S phase of interphase.

Results table. Side length of cube / cm: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Time to become colourless / s, trial 1: 17, 71, 161, 297, 430; trial 2: 17, 72, 158, 172, 429; trial 3: 19, 70, 165, 287, 451. (a) Calculate the mean time to become colourless at 2 cm, ignoring any anomalous result. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.

items.stem: Daniel spread a culture of bacteria evenly on nutrient agar plates and placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on them. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 14, 18, 24, 28, 36; trial 2: 14, 19, 24, 29, 34; trial 3: 14, 18, 24, 29, 34. items.answer: A line graph: antibiotic concentration on the x-axis and mean diameter of clear zone on the y-axis.

items.stem: E. coli with only ¹⁵N DNA is grown in ¹⁴N for two generations. What fraction of DNA molecules is hybrid?
items.answer: One half
items.markingKey: Two of four molecules are hybrid.

items.stem: In a capillary in the leg, the hydrostatic pressure is 4.8 kPa at the arterial end and 1.5 kPa at the venous end. The oncotic pressure due to plasma proteins is 3.4 kPa along the whole capillary. (a) Calculate the net pressure at each end and state the direction of fluid movement. (b) Explain why the oncotic pressure stays almost the same along the capillary.
items.answer: (a) Arterial end: 1.4 kPa outwards (fluid leaves); venous end: 1.9 kPa inwards (fluid returns). (b) Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the capillary wall, so their concentration in the blood stays high.
items.markingKey: (a) 4.8 − 3.4 = 1.4 kPa out [1]; 3.4 − 1.5 = 1.9 kPa in [1]; directions [1] (b) proteins too large to leave [1] [4]

items.answer: Triglycerides contain glycerol plus three fatty acids; they are not made of repeating monomers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Triglycerides contain glycerol plus three fatty acids; they are not made of repeating monomers. [2]

items.stem: A scientist in Kathmandu examines a cell grown from a throat swab with an electron microscope and records: no membrane-bound organelles; circular DNA free in the cytoplasm; ribosomes. State whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give two reasons from the observations.
items.answer: Prokaryotic: no membrane-bound organelles; circular DNA free in the cytoplasm.
items.markingKey: prokaryotic [1]; two correct reasons from the observations (not the shared feature) [2] [3]

items.stem: A child in Singapore is infected with measles virus for the first time. (a) Describe how B cells respond to the virus. (b) Explain why the child is unlikely to suffer from the disease if infected again.
items.answer: (a) B cell with complementary receptor binds antigen; clonal selection and expansion (mitosis); plasma cells secrete antibodies; memory cells formed. (b) Memory cells give a fast, large secondary response, destroying the virus before symptoms develop (active immunity).
items.markingKey: (a) B cell with complementary receptor binds antigen [1]; clonal selection and expansion (mitosis) [1]; plasma cells secrete antibodies [1]; memory cells formed [1] [4] (b) any 2 from: Memory cells give a fast; large secondary response; destroying the virus before symptoms develop (active immunity) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: The activation energy for the hydrolysis of a peptide is 150 kJ mol⁻¹ without a catalyst and 43 kJ mol⁻¹ with an enzyme. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in activation energy. (b) Sketch or describe an energy-level diagram for the reaction with and without the enzyme. (c) Explain how the enzyme lowers the activation energy.
items.answer: (a) 71.3% (b) Same starting and end energy levels; the enzyme curve has a lower peak; activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak. (c) The substrate binds to the active site forming an enzyme–substrate complex; induced fit strains bonds or holds reactants together so bonds break / form more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) (150 − 43) ÷ 150 × 100 = 71.3% [2] (b) lower peak with enzyme [1]; same energy of reactants / products [1] (c) E–S complex [1]; strain / orientation [1] [6]

items.stem: Priya set up a bubble potometer with a leafy shoot and measured the distance moved by an air bubble along a capillary tube (radius 0.5 mm) in 5 minutes at different wind speeds produced by a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / cm: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. Distance moved by bubble in 5 min / mm, trial 1: 39, 28, 24, 22, 20; trial 2: 40, 29, 25, 33, 21; trial 3: 40, 31, 26, 23, 20. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (c) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis. (d) Calculate the volume of water taken up per minute at the closest distance, using volume = πr² × distance.
items.answer: (a) Independent: distance from fan; dependent: distance moved by bubble in 5 min. (b) The same leafy shoot (same leaf area); light intensity. (c) A line graph: distance from fan on the x-axis and mean distance moved by bubble in 5 min on the y-axis. (d) 6.23 mm³ min⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = distance from fan [1]; dependent variable = distance moved by bubble in 5 min [1] [2] (b) Any two from: the same leafy shoot (same leaf area); light intensity; temperature; humidity; time of measurement [2] (c) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; distance from fan on x-axis and distance moved by bubble in 5 min on y-axis [1] [2] (d) π × 0.5² × 39.7 = 31.15 mm³ [1]; ÷ 5 = 6.23 mm³ min⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Researchers in Kuala Lumpur analysed the cell surface membrane of a bacterium from a hot spring and compared its phospholipids and cholesterol content with those of a related species from a temperate climate. (a) Suggest how the fatty acids in the phospholipids might differ in a cold-adapted organism, and explain why. (b) Explain why the membrane is partially permeable. (c) Describe one way to show that membranes become more permeable at high temperatures.
items.answer: (a) More unsaturated fatty acids (kinks) so phospholipids pack less tightly and the membrane stays fluid at low temperatures. (b) Hydrophobic core lets small non-polar molecules through but blocks ions / polar molecules, which need specific proteins. (c) Beetroot discs in water at different temperatures; measure pigment leakage with a colorimeter.

items.stem: An athlete in Riyadh uses about 70 kg of ATP per day, but the body contains only about 50 g of ATP at any one time. (a) Describe the structure of ATP. (b) Calculate how many times each ATP molecule is recycled per day, on average. (c) Give three uses of ATP in muscle cells.
items.answer: (a) Adenine + ribose (adenosine) + three phosphate groups. (b) 1400 (c) Contraction (myosin heads); active transport of Ca²⁺; protein synthesis; glycogen synthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) Adenine + ribose (adenosine) + three phosphate groups [2] [2] (b) 70 × 1000 ÷ 50 = 1400 [1] (c) any 3 from: Contraction (myosin heads); active transport of Ca²⁺; protein synthesis; glycogen synthesis (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: In a pressure trace from the left side of the heart of a person in Dhaka, at 0.2 s the ventricular pressure rises above the atrial pressure; at 0.25 s it rises above the aortic pressure (about 10.5 kPa); the ventricular pressure peaks at 16.7 kPa and the aortic pressure peaks at 16.3 kPa; at 0.55 s the ventricular pressure falls below the aortic pressure. (a) Calculate the time during which blood is ejected into the aorta. (b) Explain why the aortic pressure rises and falls less steeply than ventricular pressure. (c) Suggest how the trace for the right ventricle would differ. (d) State the name of the phase when both valves are closed and ventricular pressure is rising.
items.answer: (a) 0.3 s (b) Elastic tissue in the aorta stretches during systole and recoils in diastole, smoothing the pressure. (c) Same timing / shape but much lower peak pressure (about a quarter), because the right ventricle has thinner walls and pumps to the lungs. (d) Isovolumetric (isovolumic) contraction, early ventricular systole.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.55 − 0.25 = 0.3 s [1] (b) Elastic tissue in the aorta stretches during systole and recoils in diastole [1]; smoothing the pressure [1] [2] (c) Same timing / shape but much lower peak pressure (about a quarter) [1]; because the right ventricle has thinner walls and pumps to the lungs [1] [2] (d) Isovolumetric (isovolumic) contraction, early ventricular systole [1]

items.stem: A food-science student in Lisbon is asked to find out which biological molecules are present in a protein bar. (a) Describe how the student would test for protein and state the positive result. (b) The Benedict's test is negative. Describe how the student could show whether a non-reducing sugar is present. (c) Describe how to test for lipid and explain why the food must not first be dissolved in water.
items.answer: (a) Add biuret reagent (or NaOH then dilute CuSO₄) to a solution of the food; blue → purple. (b) Boil with dilute HCl, cool, neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate, heat with Benedict's solution; brick-red precipitate = non-reducing sugar present. (c) Shake with ethanol, decant into water: white emulsion. Lipid is insoluble in water so it would not dissolve and be extracted.
items.markingKey: (a) Add biuret reagent (or NaOH then dilute CuSO₄) to a solution of the food [1]; blue → purple [1] [2] (b) any 3 from: Boil with dilute HCl; cool; neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate; heat with Benedict's solution; brick-red precipitate = non-reducing sugar present (1 mark each) [3] (c) Shake with ethanol [1]; decant into water: white emulsion [1]; Lipid is insoluble in water so it would not dissolve and be extracted [1] [3]

items.stem: Researchers in Lisbon supplied a salivary gland cell with radioactively labelled amino acids for 5 minutes and then tracked the radioactivity as the cell made and secreted amylase. (a) Explain why the radioactivity first appears in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. (b) Describe how amylase leaves the cell. (c) Suggest why this cell contains many mitochondria.
items.answer: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER, and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen. (b) By exocytosis: secretory vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing the contents; this requires ATP. (c) To provide ATP for protein synthesis, vesicle movement and exocytosis.
items.markingKey: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER [1]; and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen [1] [2] (b) vesicles fuse with membrane [1]; exocytosis / ATP [1] [2] (c) To provide ATP for protein synthesis [1]; vesicle movement and exocytosis [1] [2]

items.stem: For each example, state the type of immunity (natural or artificial, active or passive) and explain whether it is long-lasting: (i) a fetus receiving antibodies across the placenta (ii) a person bitten by a snake given antivenom.
items.answer: (i) Natural passive: IgG antibodies cross from the mother; no memory cells are made; short-lived (no memory cells; antibodies broken down). (ii) Artificial passive: ready-made antibodies are injected; no memory cells are made; short-lived (no memory cells; antibodies broken down).
items.markingKey: (i) type [1]; duration with reason [1] (ii) type [1]; duration with reason [1] [4]

items.stem: A researcher in Karachi extracts the main polysaccharide from cotton fibres and finds that it is cellulose. (a) Explain how the structure of cellulose gives plant cell walls their strength. (b) Explain why humans cannot digest cellulose.
items.answer: (a) β-glucose with alternate units inverted forms straight chains; many hydrogen bonds link parallel chains into microfibrils; microfibrils in layers give high tensile strength. (b) Humans do not produce cellulase; the β 1,4 glycosidic bonds do not fit the active site of amylase.
items.markingKey: (a) β-glucose / straight chains [1]; hydrogen bonds between chains [1]; microfibrils / tensile strength [1] [3] (b) no cellulase [1]; amylase specific to α bonds [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha measured the initial rate of an enzyme reaction (μmol min⁻¹) at different substrate concentrations (mmol dm⁻³), with and without substance X. Substrate concentration: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Rate without X: 25, 40, 57.1, 72.7, 84.2, 91.4. Rate with X: 10, 16, 22.9, 29.1, 33.7, 36.6. items.stem: A patient in Lisbon has smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 10 years and now has chronic bronchitis. (a) Calculate the total number of cigarettes smoked (assume 365 days per year). (b) Describe the normal roles of goblet cells and cilia. (c) Explain how smoking leads to chronic bronchitis.
items.answer: (a) 54,750 (b) Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles and pathogens; cilia beat to move mucus up to the throat. (c) Tar paralyses / destroys cilia; goblet cells and mucous glands enlarge and produce more mucus; mucus accumulates and bacteria multiply; inflammation; airways narrow; persistent cough.

items.stem: A farmer in Mumbai removed a ring of bark (including the phloem) from the trunk of an apple tree. After some weeks, the bark above the ring swelled and the roots began to die, but the leaves did not wilt. (a) Explain why the bark above the ring swelled. (b) Explain why the leaves did not wilt. (c) Describe the mass flow hypothesis for translocation.
items.answer: (a) Sucrose from leaves (source) moving down in phloem accumulated above the ring; water entered by osmosis; cells grew. (b) Xylem (inside the phloem, in the wood) was intact, so water continued to move up. (c) Loading at source lowers ψ; water enters; high hydrostatic pressure; unloading at sink; flow down pressure gradient.

items.stem: A tumour in a patient in Mumbai was estimated to contain 50,000 cells at diagnosis, and the cells doubled every 2 days. (a) Calculate the number of cells after 6 days if untreated. (b) State the type of cell division involved and explain why the cells are genetically identical.
items.answer: (a) 400,000 (b) Mitosis: DNA replicated, then sister chromatids separated equally into each daughter nucleus.

items.stem: Oestrogen acts on cells of the uterus lining. (a) Explain whether its receptor is on the cell surface or inside the cell. (b) Outline how binding of oestrogen leads to a response.

items.stem: Health workers are planning a programme to reduce tuberculosis (TB) in a refugee camp near Cox's Bazar. (a) Suggest and explain three measures that could be included. (b) Describe how the success of the programme could be measured.
items.answer: (a) BCG vaccination: gives immunity (especially to children), so fewer people develop TB and spread it. Contact tracing and isolating infected people: infectious people are found and treated, so they do not spread droplets to others. Long courses of several antibiotics (DOTS): kill Mycobacterium completely and reduce the chance of resistance; observed treatment makes sure the course is completed. (b) Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after, over several years, compared with a similar area.
items.markingKey: (a) three measures, each explained [3] (b) any 2 from: Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after; over several years; compared with a similar area (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Biologists in Lima compared the oxygen dissociation curve of the haemoglobin of a fetus in the uterus with that of adult human haemoglobin. The curve for a fetus in the uterus lies to the left of the human curve. (a) Explain why the dissociation curve is sigmoid. (b) Describe how carbon dioxide is transported from respiring tissues to the lungs.
items.answer: (a) Cooperative binding: once one O₂ binds, Hb changes shape, making it easier for the next to bind; fourth binds less easily. (b) Mostly as HCO₃⁻ in plasma (carbonic anhydrase in red cells, chloride shift); some as carbaminohaemoglobin; some dissolved.

items.stem: Collagen is a fibrous protein that gives strength to tendons and skin. A student in Kathmandu researches how its structure relates to its function. (a) Describe what is meant by the primary, secondary and tertiary structure of a protein. (b) Name the four types of bond or interaction that stabilise tertiary structure. (c) Suggest the effect on the function of collagen of heating it to 80 °C.
items.answer: (a) Primary: amino acid sequence; secondary: α-helix / β-pleated sheet held by H-bonds between backbone groups; tertiary: 3-D folding held by bonds between R groups. (b) Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds, hydrophobic interactions. (c) Hydrogen and ionic bonds break, so the 3-D shape is lost (denatured); it can no longer carry out its function.

options: Monocytes that leave the blood and enter tissues
items.answer: Monocytes that leave the blood and enter tissues

items.stem: During exercise, the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin shifts to the right. Which explains this?
options: Haemoglobin binds carbon dioxide at the haem group
Higher carbon dioxide concentration lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen
Less carbonic anhydrase in red cells
Higher oxygen concentration in the muscles
items.answer: Higher carbon dioxide concentration lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen
items.markingKey: Bohr shift.

items.stem: A cell surface membrane appears 2.5 mm thick in an electron micrograph at ×250,000. What is its actual thickness?
items.answer: 10 nm

items.stem: Arjun writes in a revision note: "Telomeres contain the most important genes." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Telomeres are non-coding repetitive sequences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Telomeres are non-coding repetitive sequences. [2]

items.stem: Felix measures the image of a ciliated epithelial cell in a micrograph as 31 mm. The magnification is ×800. Calculate the actual length of a ciliated epithelial cell, giving your answer in micrometres (μm).
State why DNA replication must be accurate.
items.answer: So that daughter cells receive identical genetic information; errors are mutations that may change proteins.
items.markingKey: So that daughter cells receive identical genetic information; errors are mutations that may change proteins [1]

items.stem: Which describes a non-competitive inhibitor?
options: It binds to a site other than the active site and changes its shape
It has the same shape as the substrate
Its effect is overcome by adding more substrate
items.answer: It binds to a site other than the active site and changes its shape
items.markingKey: Increasing substrate does not overcome it; Vmax is lowered.

items.stem: A student in Madrid states: "Antibiotics can cure flu." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Flu is caused by a virus; antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

items.stem: Sipho carried out a semi-quantitative Benedict's test. Standard glucose solutions of 0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 % gave the colours blue, green, yellow, orange, red-orange, brick red respectively. A urine sample gave a colour between green and yellow. Explain why the colours give only a semi-quantitative estimate.
items.answer: Judging colour is subjective and colours between standards cannot be measured; only a range can be given.
items.markingKey: Judging colour is subjective and colours between standards cannot be measured [1]; only a range can be given [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the clumping together of pathogens by antibodies, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf"?
items.answer: Agglutination
items.markingKey: Agglutination: the clumping together of pathogens by antibodies, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf.

items.stem: When do the semilunar valves open?
options: When atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
When ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the arteries
items.answer: When ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the arteries
items.markingKey: Blood is then ejected into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

items.stem: Cell X has ψ = −400 kPa and cell Y has ψ = −700 kPa. Which statement is correct?
options: Solutes move from X to Y by osmosis
Water moves from Y to X by osmosis
There is no net movement of water
Water moves from X to Y by osmosis
items.answer: Water moves from X to Y by osmosis
items.markingKey: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower water potential.

items.stem: A student in Accra states: "Cancer cells divide by meiosis." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Cancer cells divide by uncontrolled mitosis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Cancer cells divide by uncontrolled mitosis. [2]

items.stem: A study in Toronto compared healthy lungs with lungs affected by emphysema. Healthy: alveolar surface area 70 m², diffusion distance 0.5 μm. Affected: surface area 37 m², diffusion distance 1.9 μm. Calculate the percentage decrease in surface area.
Mohammed says: "tRNA molecules carry the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome." Explain whether Mohammed is correct.
items.answer: mRNA carries the code; tRNA brings specific amino acids.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: mRNA carries the code; tRNA brings specific amino acids. [2]

items.stem: The activation energy for the hydrolysis of sucrose is 86 kJ mol⁻¹ without a catalyst and 22 kJ mol⁻¹ with an enzyme. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in activation energy. (b) Sketch or describe an energy-level diagram for the reaction with and without the enzyme. (c) Explain how the enzyme lowers the activation energy.
items.answer: (a) 74.4% (b) Same starting and end energy levels; the enzyme curve has a lower peak; activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak. (c) The substrate binds to the active site forming an enzyme–substrate complex; induced fit strains bonds or holds reactants together so bonds break / form more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) (86 − 22) ÷ 86 × 100 = 74.4% [2] (b) lower peak with enzyme [1]; same energy of reactants / products [1] (c) E–S complex [1]; strain / orientation [1] [6]

items.stem: The basic reproduction number (R₀) of mumps is about 7. (a) Calculate the herd immunity threshold using (1 − 1/R₀) × 100. (b) The vaccine is 93% effective. Calculate the vaccination coverage needed to reach the threshold.
Which process creates the high hydrostatic pressure at the source end of a sieve tube?
options: Active transport of water into sieve tubes
Water entering by osmosis after sucrose is actively loaded
items.answer: Water entering by osmosis after sucrose is actively loaded
items.markingKey: Loading lowers ψ.

items.stem: A spherical bacterium (coccus) has a diameter of 1.9 μm and a spherical eukaryotic cell has a diameter of 15 μm. (a) Calculate how many times larger the diameter of the eukaryotic cell is. (b) Using V = 4/3 πr³, calculate how many times larger its volume is.
items.markingKey: (a) 15 ÷ 1.9 = 7.9 [1] (b) volumes 1770 μm³ and 3.59 μm³ [1]; ratio 492 (= ratio of diameters cubed) [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Nairobi states: "Hydrogen bonds are strong covalent bonds within water molecules." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between water molecules; the bonds within a molecule are covalent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between water molecules; the bonds within a molecule are covalent. [2]

items.stem: A volunteer in Jakarta was injected with an antigen on day 0 and again on day 42. After the first injection, antibody was first detected after 8 days and peaked at 10 arbitrary units. After the second injection, antibody was detected after 3 days and peaked at 200 arbitrary units. (a) Calculate how many times greater the peak concentration was after the second injection. (b) Suggest why the antibody concentration falls after each peak.
items.answer: (a) 20 (b) Antigen has been removed so plasma cells stop secreting / die; antibodies are broken down.
items.markingKey: (a) 200 ÷ 10 = 20 [1] (b) Antigen has been removed so plasma cells stop secreting / die [1]; antibodies are broken down [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the structure of a vein and an artery, and relate each difference to the function of the vessel.
items.answer: Vein: thin wall with little elastic tissue and muscle; wide lumen; valves; it carries blood back to the heart at low pressure; valves prevent backflow. Artery: thick wall with much elastic tissue and smooth muscle; narrow lumen; no valves (except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery); it carries blood away from the heart at high pressure; elastic recoil smooths flow.
items.markingKey: three structural differences [3]; each linked to function [1] [4]

items.stem: A cube of side 3 cm is cut into 27 cubes of side 1 cm. What happens to the total surface area to volume ratio?
items.answer: It increases from 2 : 1 to 6 : 1
items.markingKey: SA:V = 6/L.

items.stem: Zara grew garlic roots in water at different temperatures, then prepared root tip squashes and counted the number of cells in mitosis out of 200 cells in each field of view. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Number of cells in mitosis (out of 200) / cells, trial 1: 2, 7, 19, 32, 39, 32; trial 2: 2, 8, 19, 30, 37, 31; trial 3: 2, 8, 11, 31, 39, 32. Calculate the mean number of cells in mitosis (out of 200) at 20 °C, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: 31 cells

items.stem: Mei says: "A substitution always causes a frameshift." Explain whether Mei is correct.
items.answer: A substitution changes only one codon; insertions and deletions cause frameshifts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: A substitution changes only one codon; insertions and deletions cause frameshifts. [2]

items.stem: Chloe mixed amylase with starch solution in buffers of different pH at 35 °C. Every 10 s a drop of the mixture was tested with iodine solution on a spotting tile, and the time taken until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. pH: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 381, 116, 36, 155, 659; trial 2: 404, 112, 35, 154, 479; trial 3: 387, 118, 35, 158, 461. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) State the uncertainty in the times recorded and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Test more frequently (e.g. every 5 s) to reduce the uncertainty in the end point. (b) ±10 s (or ±5 s): samples were tested only every 10 s, so the end point lies between two tests.
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: test more frequently (e.g. every 5 s) to reduce the uncertainty in the end point; use a colorimeter to judge the end point objectively; use a narrower range of pH near the optimum; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the pH (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) ±10 s [1]; sampling interval [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel examined a transverse section of a privet (Ligustrum) leaf with a light microscope and made a low-power plan diagram. (a) Describe the distribution of xylem and phloem in this organ. (b) Explain how the stain toluidine blue or phloroglucinol helps to identify xylem. (c) The image of a xylem vessel is 12 mm wide at ×200. Calculate its actual width.
items.answer: (a) Stem: vascular bundles in a ring, xylem inside, phloem outside. Root: central xylem (star / X shape) with phloem between the arms. Leaf: xylem upper, phloem lower in the midrib. (b) Lignin stains differently (red with phloroglucinol / blue-green with toluidine blue), so lignified xylem is distinguished. (c) 60 μm
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Stem: vascular bundles in a ring, xylem inside, phloem outside; Root: central xylem (star / X shape) with phloem between the arms; Leaf: xylem upper, phloem lower in the midrib (1 mark each) [2] (b) Lignin stains differently (red with phloroglucinol / blue-green with toluidine blue) [1]; so lignified xylem is distinguished [1] [2] (c) 12 mm = 12 000 μm; ÷ 200 = 60 μm [2]

items.stem: Mei measures the image of a bacteriophage T4 in a micrograph as 38 mm. The magnification is ×200,000. Calculate the actual length of a bacteriophage T4, giving your answer in nanometres (nm).
items.answer: 190 nm

items.stem: Keratin is a fibrous protein that forms hair and nails. A student in Nairobi researches how its structure relates to its function. (a) Explain why keratin is described as fibrous. (b) Name the four types of bond or interaction that stabilise tertiary structure. (c) Suggest the effect on the function of keratin of heating it to 80 °C. (d) Describe how a peptide bond is formed.
items.answer: (a) Fibrous: long parallel chains, insoluble, repetitive sequence, structural role. (b) Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds, hydrophobic interactions. (c) Hydrogen and ionic bonds break, so the 3-D shape is lost (denatured); it can no longer carry out its function. (d) Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next, removing water and forming –CO–NH–.
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Fibrous: long parallel chains; insoluble; repetitive sequence; structural role (1 mark each) [2] (b) four [2]; two or three [1] [2] (c) Hydrogen and ionic bonds break, so the 3-D shape is lost (denatured) [1]; it can no longer carry out its function [1] [2] (d) Condensation between –COOH of one amino acid and –NH₂ of the next [1]; removing water and forming –CO–NH– [1] [2]

items.stem: A vaccination campaign in Bogotá uses a measles vaccine containing attenuated (weakened) live virus. (a) Explain how the vaccine gives long-term protection. (b) Explain why it is important that a high percentage of the population is vaccinated.
items.answer: (a) Antigens stimulate B and T cells with complementary receptors; clonal selection and expansion; plasma cells make antibodies; memory cells remain and give a fast secondary response on infection. (b) Herd immunity: too few susceptible people for the pathogen to spread, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
items.markingKey: (a) Antigens stimulate B and T cells with complementary receptors [1]; clonal selection and expansion [1]; plasma cells make antibodies [1]; memory cells remain and give a fast secondary response on infection [1] [4] (b) Herd immunity: too few susceptible people for the pathogen to spread [1]; protecting those who cannot be vaccinated [1] [2]

items.stem: A doctor in Accra studies the ECG of a patient and notices that the QRS complexes are wide and irregular and very rapid. (a) Suggest what is happening in the patient's heart. (b) Describe how a heartbeat is normally initiated and coordinated.
items.answer: (a) Ventricles are contracting abnormally (ventricular fibrillation). (b) SAN in right atrium sends wave of excitation over atria (contract); non-conducting tissue; AVN delays; Purkyne tissue in septum to apex; ventricles contract from base upwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Ventricles are contracting abnormally (ventricular fibrillation) [2] [2] (b) any 4 from: SAN in right atrium sends wave of excitation over atria (contract); non-conducting tissue; AVN delays; Purkyne tissue in septum to apex; ventricles contract from base upwards (1 mark each) [4]

items.stem: Glucagon acts on liver cells. (a) Explain whether its receptor is on the cell surface or inside the cell. (b) Outline how binding of glucagon leads to a response.
items.answer: (a) On the cell surface: it is water-soluble and cannot cross the bilayer. (b) It binds a surface receptor, activating a G protein and adenylyl cyclase to make cyclic AMP, which activates enzymes that break down glycogen.
items.markingKey: (a) location with reason [2] (b) binding to specific receptor [1]; transduction / response [1] [4]

items.stem: A researcher in Nairobi extracts the main polysaccharide from wheat endosperm and finds that it is starch. (a) Describe how two α-glucose molecules join together by a condensation reaction. (b) Describe how to test the extract for starch and state the expected result. (c) Compare the structure of glycogen with that of cellulose.
items.answer: (a) Condensation between the OH on C1 of one glucose and the OH on C4 of the other; water removed; 1,4 glycosidic bond formed. (b) Add iodine in potassium iodide solution: orange-brown to blue-black. (c) Glycogen: α-glucose, 1,4 and 1,6 bonds, highly branched, compact. Cellulose: β-glucose, 1,4 bonds only, straight chains, hydrogen bonds between chains forming microfibrils.
items.markingKey: (a) C1 and C4 [1]; water removed [1]; 1,4 glycosidic bond [1] [3] (b) iodine solution [1]; correct colour [1] [2] (c) two differences [2]; one similarity (glucose / glycosidic bonds / polysaccharide) [1] [3]

items.stem: A patient in Hanoi has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 10 years and now has chronic bronchitis. (a) Describe the normal roles of goblet cells and cilia. (b) Explain how smoking leads to chronic bronchitis. (c) Suggest why the patient is at greater risk of lung infections.
items.answer: (a) Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles and pathogens; cilia beat to move mucus up to the throat. (b) Tar paralyses / destroys cilia; goblet cells and mucous glands enlarge and produce more mucus; mucus accumulates and bacteria multiply; inflammation; airways narrow; persistent cough. (c) Pathogens trapped in mucus are not removed and can multiply.
items.markingKey: (a) Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles and pathogens [1]; cilia beat to move mucus up to the throat [1] [2] (b) any 3 from: Tar paralyses / destroys cilia; goblet cells and mucous glands enlarge and produce more mucus; mucus accumulates and bacteria multiply; inflammation; airways narrow; persistent cough (1 mark each) [3] (c) Pathogens trapped in mucus are not removed and can multiply [1]

items.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule from yeast contains 2,400 base pairs, and 29% of its bases are adenine. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases. (b) Calculate the number of cytosine bases in the molecule. (c) Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds between the bases.

A biotechnology company in Dubai compares two enzymes that act on glucose: hexokinase (Km = 0.5 mmol dm⁻³) and glucokinase (Km = 5.0 mmol dm⁻³). Both have similar Vmax values. (a) State which enzyme has the higher affinity for the substrate and explain your answer. (b) Describe how Km could be found from experimental data.
items.answer: (a) Hexokinase: lower Km, so half Vmax is reached at a lower substrate concentration. (b) Measure initial rates at a range of substrate concentrations; plot rate against concentration; find Vmax from plateau; Km = substrate concentration at ½Vmax.
items.markingKey: (a) Hexokinase: lower Km [1]; so half Vmax is reached at a lower substrate concentration [1] [2] (b) any 3 from: Measure initial rates at a range of substrate concentrations; plot rate against concentration; find Vmax from plateau; Km = substrate concentration at ½Vmax (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: A health ministry recorded 1,996 new cases of cholera in 2020 and 1,269 in 2024 in a region with a population of 5,000,000 (assume constant). (a) Calculate the incidence per 100 000 people in each year. (b) Calculate the percentage change in incidence. (c) Describe how cholera is transmitted and suggest one reason for the change.
items.answer: (a) 39.9 and 25.4 per 100 000 (b) −36.4% (a decrease) (c) Drinking water or eating food contaminated with faeces from infected people. Possible reason for the fall: better control, e.g. provide clean, treated (chlorinated) drinking water.

items.stem: A plant physiologist in Nairobi supplied a dye that moves only through cell walls to the roots of a tomato plant. The dye was found in the walls of cortex cells but stopped at the endodermis. (a) Explain the advantage to the plant of the Casparian strip. (b) Describe the symplast pathway. (c) Suggest why the diameter of the trunk of a tree decreases slightly during the day.
items.answer: (a) Water and ions must pass through cell surface membranes / cytoplasm, so the plant controls which ions enter xylem; prevents back-flow; allows root pressure. (b) Water moves through cytoplasm of cells, from cell to cell via plasmodesmata, by osmosis. (c) Tension in xylem during high transpiration pulls vessel walls inwards slightly.
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Water and ions must pass through cell surface membranes / cytoplasm, so the plant controls which ions enter xylem; prevents back-flow; allows root pressure (1 mark each) [2] (b) any 2 from: Water moves through cytoplasm of cells; from cell to cell via plasmodesmata; by osmosis (1 mark each) [2] (c) Tension in xylem during high transpiration pulls vessel walls inwards slightly [2] [2]

items.stem: Researchers in Doha supplied a goblet cell with radioactively labelled amino acids for 10 minutes and then tracked the radioactivity as the cell made and secreted mucin (a glycoprotein). (a) State, in order, the organelles in which the radioactivity would appear. (b) Describe how mucin (a glycoprotein) leaves the cell. (c) Explain why the cell would also contain a large nucleolus.
items.answer: (a) Ribosomes on RER → RER cisternae → transport vesicles → Golgi body → secretory vesicles → (outside cell). (b) By exocytosis: secretory vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing the contents; this requires ATP. (c) The nucleolus makes ribosomes; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) RER [1]; Golgi [1]; secretory vesicles [1] [3] (b) vesicles fuse with membrane [1]; exocytosis / ATP [1] [2] (c) The nucleolus makes ribosomes [1]; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Respiration of lipid releases about 39 kJ g⁻¹ and of carbohydrate about 16 kJ g⁻¹. A desert camel needs to store 2000 kJ of energy. (a) Calculate the mass of lipid and of carbohydrate needed. (b) Calculate the mass saved by storing lipid. (c) Explain why lipid is a better energy store for a desert camel.
items.answer: (a) lipid 51.3 g; carbohydrate 125 g (b) 73.7 g (c) Lipid releases more than twice as much energy per gram, so less mass is carried; it is insoluble and also releases metabolic water / provides insulation.
items.markingKey: (a) 2000 ÷ 39 = 51.3 g [1]; 2000 ÷ 16 = 125 g [1] (b) 73.7 g [1] (c) more energy per gram / less mass [1]; extra benefit (metabolic water / insulation / buoyancy) [1] [5]

items.stem: Elena examined a stained blood smear and counted 400 white blood cells: neutrophils 263, lymphocytes 114, monocytes 18, others 5. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of neutrophils and lymphocytes. (b) The total white cell count is 15 × 10⁹ dm⁻³. Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³. (c) Describe how you would distinguish a neutrophil from a lymphocyte in the smear.
items.answer: (a) neutrophils 65.8%; lymphocytes 28.5% (b) 9.86 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (c) Neutrophil: lobed nucleus, granular cytoplasm, larger (10–12 μm). Lymphocyte: large round nucleus filling most of the cell, little cytoplasm, smaller (about 7 μm).
items.markingKey: (a) 263 ÷ 400 × 100 = 65.8% [1]; 114 ÷ 400 × 100 = 28.5% [1] (b) 0.657 × 15 × 10⁹ = 9.86 × 10⁹ [2] (c) neutrophil lobed nucleus [1]; lymphocyte large round nucleus / little cytoplasm [1] [6]

items.stem: Biologists in Lagos compared the oxygen dissociation curve of the haemoglobin of a fetus in the uterus with that of adult human haemoglobin. The curve for a fetus in the uterus lies to the left of the human curve. (a) Explain what this tells you about the affinity of this haemoglobin for oxygen. (b) Explain the Bohr shift.
items.answer: (a) Higher affinity (left) – more saturated at a given pO₂. (b) More CO₂ → more H⁺ → binds Hb → lower affinity → curve shifts right → more O₂ released where CO₂ is high.
items.markingKey: (a) Higher affinity (left) – more saturated at a given pO₂ [2] [2] (b) any 3 from: More CO₂; more H⁺; binds Hb; lower affinity; curve shifts right; more O₂ released where CO₂ is high (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Noah cut equal-sized discs of beetroot, washed them, and placed them in distilled water for 30 minutes at different temperatures. The absorbance of the water (caused by red betalain pigment that leaked from the cells) was measured with a colorimeter. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 25, 40, 55, 70. Absorbance / arbitrary units, trial 1: 0.05, 0.06, 0.14, 0.68, 0.97; trial 2: 0.05, 0.06, 0.2, 0.64, 0.96; trial 3: 0.06, 0.06, 0.13, 0.69, 0.97. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (c) Explain why the colorimeter is set to zero (calibrated) using distilled water before readings are taken.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: absorbance. (b) Number, size and surface area of beetroot discs; volume of distilled water. (c) So that the absorbance recorded is due only to pigment in the solution, not the water or the cuvette.

items.stem: A karyotype prepared from a dividing cell of a potato in a laboratory in Lima shows 48 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, arranged in 24 homologous pairs. (a) State the stage of the cell cycle at which the cells were most likely stopped, and explain why. (b) Explain the meaning of homologous chromosomes. (c) Explain why telomeres are present at the ends of the chromosomes.
items.answer: (a) Metaphase: chromosomes are most condensed and visible, each with two chromatids. (b) Same genes at the same loci; one maternal and one paternal; same size and centromere position (may have different alleles). (c) Non-coding repeats lost at each replication instead of genes; protect chromosome ends.

items.stem: Yusuf, a student in Lagos, examined prepared slides of transverse sections of the trachea, a bronchiole and alveolar tissue with a light microscope. (a) Explain how the structure of the alveolar wall is related to its function. (b) An alveolus has an image diameter of 50 mm at ×200. Calculate its actual diameter in μm. (c) State the function of goblet cells and cilia.
items.answer: (a) Squamous epithelium one cell thick – short diffusion distance; elastic fibres for recoil; close contact with capillaries. (b) 250 μm (c) Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles; cilia beat to move mucus up to the throat.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "leading strand"?
options: DNA replication in which each new molecule contains one strand from the original molecule and one newly synthesised strand.
The new strand synthesised discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments, away from the replication fork.
The enzyme that breaks hydrogen bonds between bases to unwind and separate the two strands of DNA.
The new strand synthesised continuously in the 5′ to 3′ direction towards the replication fork.
items.answer: The new strand synthesised continuously in the 5′ to 3′ direction towards the replication fork.
items.markingKey: Leading strand: the new strand synthesised continuously in the 5′ to 3′ direction towards the replication fork.

items.answer: Bronchiole

items.answer: Secretion of proteins

items.stem: A leaf of a bean plant was supplied with ¹⁴CO₂. Radioactive sucrose was detected in an aphid stylet 45 cm below the leaf after 60 minutes. (a) Calculate the rate of translocation in mm min⁻¹. (b) Explain how the ¹⁴C came to be in sucrose in the phloem. (c) Explain why aphid stylets are useful in investigating translocation.
items.answer: (a) 7.5 mm min⁻¹ (b) ¹⁴CO₂ was fixed in photosynthesis into sugars, converted to sucrose and loaded into phloem at the source. (c) The stylet penetrates a single sieve tube, so pure phloem sap can be collected and analysed (and pressure shown by sap exuding).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why increasing the substrate concentration overcomes competitive inhibition but not non-competitive inhibition. (b) Explain how end-product inhibition controls a metabolic pathway.
items.answer: (a) Competitive inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site; more substrate means more likely to bind than the inhibitor. (b) The end product binds (non-competitively, at an allosteric site) to an enzyme early in the pathway, reducing its activity; when the product is used up, the inhibition is removed. This prevents waste of resources.

(d) Explain why the colorimeter is set to zero (calibrated) using distilled water before readings are taken.
items.answer: (a) At low temperatures little pigment leaks out. (b) Use a cork borer and blade to cut discs of identical size. (c) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean absorbance on the y-axis. (d) So that the absorbance recorded is due only to pigment in the solution, not the water or the cuvette.

(a) Calculate the time taken for mucus to travel the length of the trachea in each person. (b) Explain the difference and suggest one consequence for the smoker.
items.answer: (a) healthy 8.3 min; smoker 30.3 min (b) Smoke paralyses / destroys cilia (and increases mucus), so mucus moves more slowly; pathogens remain longer in the airways, increasing infections (bronchitis) and coughing.

items.stem: A eukaryotic gene contains 3 exons of 360, 360, 150 base pairs and 2 introns of 600, 600 base pairs. (a) Calculate the length of the primary transcript and of the mature mRNA. (b) Assuming the mature mRNA contains only coding codons and one stop codon, calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
items.answer: (a) primary 2,070 nucleotides; mature 870 nucleotides (b) 289

items.stem: Health workers are planning a programme to reduce measles in a flooded district in Sindh. (a) Suggest and explain three measures that could be included. (b) Describe how the success of the programme could be measured.
items.answer: (a) Vaccination (MMR) with high coverage: gives individual immunity and herd immunity so the virus cannot spread. Isolating infected people: prevents droplet transmission to susceptible people. Vitamin A supplements for children: reduce the severity of the disease and deaths, though not transmission. (b) Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after, over several years, compared with a similar area.
items.markingKey: (a) three measures, each explained [3] (b) any 2 from: Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after; over several years; compared with a similar area (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: A triglyceride is formed from glycerol (Mr 92) and three fatty acids: stearic acid (Mr 284), lauric acid (Mr 200), linoleic acid (Mr 280). (a) State the number of ester bonds and of water molecules released. (b) Calculate the Mr of the triglyceride (Mr of water = 18). (c) Predict whether this triglyceride is more likely to be a fat or an oil at room temperature, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 3 ester bonds; 3 water molecules (b) 802 (c) An oil (liquid): unsaturated fatty acids have kinks, so molecules cannot pack closely, lowering the melting point.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 and 3 [1] (b) 92 + 284 + 200 + 280 = 856 [1]; − 54 = 802 [1] (c) correct prediction [1]; kinks / packing explanation [1] [5]

items.stem: Tomás cut cubes of agar containing phenolphthalein and sodium hydroxide (pink) with different side lengths, placed them in 1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and timed how long each took to become colourless. Results table. Side length of cube / cm: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Time to become colourless / s, trial 1: 18, 69, 154, 281, 443; trial 2: 17, 70, 158, 277, 254; trial 3: 17, 73, 159, 271, 442. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (c) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Independent: side length of cube; dependent: time to become colourless. (b) Trial 2 at 2.5 cm (254 s); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (c) A line graph: side length of cube on the x-axis and mean time to become colourless on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = side length of cube [1]; dependent variable = time to become colourless [1] [2] (b) trial 2 at 2.5 cm identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (c) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; side length of cube on x-axis and time to become colourless on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: A transmission electron micrograph of Escherichia coli at ×20,000 shows a cell wall, a capsule, a circular DNA molecule, plasmids, 70S ribosomes and a flagellum. The cell is 50 mm long in the micrograph. (a) Calculate the actual length of the cell in μm. (b) State the function of the capsule. (c) Explain why the bacterium is classified as a prokaryote. (d) Suggest why the presence of plasmids may make infections with this bacterium more difficult to treat.
items.answer: (a) 2.5 μm (b) Protects the bacterium (from phagocytosis / drying out) and helps it stick to surfaces. (c) It has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm. (d) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria.
items.markingKey: (a) 50 mm = 50000 μm; ÷ 20,000 = 2.5 μm [2] (b) Protects the bacterium (from phagocytosis / drying out) and helps it stick to surfaces [1] (c) It has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles [1]; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm [1] [2] (d) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria [2] [2]

items.stem: In cultured human fibroblasts, telomeres start at about 8,000 base pairs and shorten by about 50 base pairs each division. Cells stop dividing when telomeres reach 3,000 base pairs. (a) Calculate the maximum number of divisions. (b) Explain why cells stop dividing when telomeres become too short.
items.answer: (a) 100 divisions (b) Further replication would lose coding DNA (genes) from the chromosome ends, so the cell stops dividing (senescence).
items.markingKey: (a) (8,000 − 3,000) ÷ 50 = 100 [2] (b) genes would be lost [1]; senescence / stops dividing [1] [4]
